subject: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)

chunks.topic: Rationale and Position in the Curriculum
chunks.content: ICT is one of nine learning areas at Junior level in Zimbabwe's reviewed Curriculum Framework. It requires learners to develop adequate life and career skills, equipping them for entry-level work, further study, lifelong learning, and life as inquisitive, reflective, discerning and caring citizens. The syllabus gives learners a broad perspective on the basic knowledge and practical skills needed to use and apply a variety of technologies in everyday life, and understand how information systems are designed and how they work. The ICT syllabus is intended to be infused within other subjects across the school curriculum, not taught in isolation.

The Junior ICT syllabus follows a spiral approach (the same topics are taught at every grade level, gaining in breadth and depth as learners progress). The 8 topics covered Grade 3-7 are: (1) ICT Tools, (2) Creating and Publishing, (3) Computer Software, (4) Safety and Security, (5) The World Wide Web and Online Collaboration, (6) ICT Enterprise, (7) Programming, and (8) Communication and Networks.

ICT is assessed through Continuous Assessment (55% of the final mark - profiling, tests and practical assignments administered and collated from Infant through to Grade 7, with research/design projects starting at Grade 5) and Summative Assessment (45%, split into Paper 1 worth 20% and Paper 2 worth 25%). By the end of Junior ICT, learners are expected to demonstrate Knowledge and Understanding (e.g. identifying ICT tools, communicating using ICT, archiving cultural information using ICT), Problem Solving (e.g. creating a computer project from a problem statement, designing data flow diagrams), and Practical Skills (e.g. developing presentations, diagnosing and repairing ICT tool faults, updating and using anti-virus software).

Grade 3: Types of Computers - learners identify and describe different types of personal computers (e.g. desktop, laptop) and match computer pictures with their names. Grade 4: Computer Peripherals - input/output devices connected to a computer. Grade 5: Fault Diagnosis and Fixing - identifying and correcting simple computer faults. Grade 6: Hardware and Software Maintenance - keeping computer hardware and software in good working order. Grade 7: Faults in ICT Tools - more advanced fault identification and troubleshooting across ICT tools generally.
learning_activities: Identifying different types of personal computers (Grade 3)
Matching computer pictures with their correct names (Grade 3)
Diagnosing and fixing simple computer faults (Grade 5)

chunks.content: Grade 3: Charts, Bar Graphs, Pictograms - creating simple visual representations of data. Grade 4: Presentations, Slide shows of drawings/images - creating basic slide-based presentations. Grade 5: Animation, Databases - introducing simple animation and basic database concepts. Grade 6: Database forms and reports - building structured database forms and generating reports. Grade 7: Database queries, Database Principles - querying databases and understanding underlying database design principles.
learning_activities: Creating charts, bar graphs and pictograms from simple data (Grade 3)
Building a basic slide show presentation with images (Grade 4)
Designing a simple database form and generating a report from it (Grade 6)

chunks.content: Grade 3: Uses of software, Text Input, File management - understanding what software does and basic typing/file organisation skills. Grade 4: Desktop Publishing, File management, Multimedia - creating simple documents/layouts and working with multimedia files. Grade 5: Sending and receiving information (VoIP), Multimedia - using Voice over Internet Protocol tools and further multimedia work. Grade 6: Spreadsheets, Data storage - working with spreadsheet software and understanding data storage concepts. Grade 7: Multimedia, Installation of software - advanced multimedia work and learning to install software programs.
learning_activities: Practising basic text input and organising files into folders (Grade 3)
Creating a simple desktop-published document (Grade 4)
Entering and organising data in a spreadsheet (Grade 6)

chunks.content: Grade 3: Passwords - understanding what a password is and why it matters for account security. Grade 4: Computer Viruses, Antivirus - learning about viruses and how antivirus software protects a computer. Grade 5: Cyber Wellness - safe, healthy and responsible use of ICT and online spaces. Grade 6: Hacking, Data Legislation - understanding what hacking is and basic awareness of laws governing data. Grade 7: Firewalls - understanding how firewalls help protect computer networks from unauthorised access.
learning_activities: Creating and explaining the importance of a strong password (Grade 3)
Discussing what computer viruses are and how antivirus software helps (Grade 4)
Discussing cyber wellness practices for safe internet use (Grade 5)

chunks.strand: 5. The World Wide Web and Online Collaboration
chunks.topic: World Wide Web and Online Collaboration - Grade-by-Grade Progression
chunks.content: Grade 3: Web page, Search Engines, Information Presentation - basic understanding of what a webpage is and how to search for information online. Grade 4: Web page, Search Tools, Information Presentation - continued development of web navigation and search skills. Grade 5: Surfing the Internet, E-mail, Mailbox, e-Messages - learning to browse the internet and use email/messaging. Grade 6: Web Page, Surfing the Internet, Web design, e-Messages - introduction to basic web design concepts. Grade 7: Surfing the Internet, Web design - more advanced internet use and web design skills.
learning_activities: Using a search engine to find information on a given topic (Grade 3)
Sending and receiving a simple email (Grade 5)
Designing a basic web page layout (Grade 6-7)

chunks.content: This topic introduces learners progressively to ICT-related careers: Grade 3 - Data capture clerk; Grade 4 - Computer Operator, Copyist; Grade 5 - Digital Photographer, Sound technician; Grade 6 - Web Developer, Software Technicians; Grade 7 - ICT Careers (broader overview), Web Designing, Network Technicians. This strand builds career awareness alongside the more technical topics, connecting classroom ICT skills to real workplace roles.
learning_activities: Learning about the role of a data capture clerk (Grade 3)
Discussing the work of a digital photographer or sound technician (Grade 5)
Researching different ICT careers such as web developer or network technician (Grade 6-7)

chunks.topic: Types and Benefits of Computer Networks (Grade 3 worked example)
chunks.content: A Grade 3 lesson on Communication and Networks (Sub-Topic: Types of Computer Networks) has learners build on their existing knowledge of social networks (e.g. WhatsApp) to identify types of computer networks, describe their characteristics, and discuss the benefits of computer networks. The lesson explicitly assumes learners already know social networking apps like WhatsApp as a starting point before introducing formal computer networking concepts.
learning_activities: Class discussion on the benefits of familiar social networks such as WhatsApp and Facebook
Grouping computer networks according to given characteristics
Identifying types of computer networks seen in an instructional video
Answering group questions on the benefits and characteristics of computer networks

chunks.content: ICT teaching methods are grouped into three categories aligned with domains of learning: Cognitive development methods (Discussion, Questioning/Socratic Method, Team Teaching, Field Trips, Group work), Affective development methods (Modelling, Simulation, Dramatic Method, Role-Playing, Observation, Lecture), and Psychomotor development methods (Inquiry Method, Interactive e-learning, Discovery Method, Demonstration, Project Method, Games, Song and dance). Teachers are encouraged to expose learners to more than one method per lesson, chosen based on the subject matter, instructional objectives, learner development level, content, time, materials, and class size.

chunks.topic: What Programming Is and Basic Concepts
chunks.content: Programming is the process of writing instructions (code) that tell a computer what to do, using a programming language. At Junior level, programming is typically introduced through visual/block-based tools (such as Scratch) rather than text-based coding, allowing learners to drag and connect coloured blocks representing commands instead of typing syntax. Core programming concepts introduced include: sequence (instructions run in a specific order, one after another), loops/repetition (repeating a set of instructions a number of times, e.g. 'repeat 10 times'), conditionals/selection (making decisions, e.g. 'if the sprite touches the edge, then bounce'), events (triggering an action when something happens, e.g. 'when green flag clicked'), and variables (storing and reusing values, e.g. a score counter). These same four building blocks (sequence, loops, conditionals, variables) underlie all programming languages, from simple block-coding tools to professional languages like Python or JavaScript.

An algorithm is a step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem or completing a task, and it is the foundation of any computer program - before writing code, a programmer typically plans out the algorithm (sometimes as a flowchart or in plain language) describing what the program should do, step by step. Debugging is the process of finding and fixing errors ('bugs') in a program. Common Junior-level debugging skills include: running the program and observing what actually happens versus what was expected, checking instructions in the correct order, checking that loop and conditional blocks are set up correctly, and testing the program after each small change rather than writing everything at once and testing only at the end.

A computer network is a group of two or more connected computers/devices that can share data, resources (like a printer) and communicate with each other. Common types include: LAN (Local Area Network - connects devices within a small area such as one school, office or home, usually via cables or Wi-Fi), WAN (Wide Area Network - connects devices over a large geographic area, potentially across cities or countries; the internet is the largest example of a WAN), and PAN (Personal Area Network - a very short-range network connecting an individual's personal devices, e.g. a phone connected to wireless earbuds via Bluetooth). Networks can be wired (using cables such as Ethernet) or wireless (using Wi-Fi, Bluetooth or mobile data signals). The benefits of computer networks include shared access to resources (printers, files, internet), easier communication, and centralised data storage/backup.

chunks.topic: The Internet vs the World Wide Web
chunks.content: The Internet and the World Wide Web (WWW) are related but different: the Internet is the vast physical/technical network of interconnected computers and cables (and wireless links) worldwide that allows data to travel between devices. The World Wide Web is a system of interlinked documents (web pages) accessed via the Internet, using a web browser (such as Chrome or Firefox) and identified by web addresses (URLs). In simple terms: the Internet is the network/infrastructure, and the Web is one of the many services that runs on top of that infrastructure (email and file transfer are other services that also run over the Internet, separate from the Web).

A password protects an account or device from unauthorised access. A strong password typically: is at least 8-12 characters long, combines uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and symbols, avoids easily guessed information (own name, birthday, 'password123'), and is different for each important account so that if one password is discovered, other accounts stay safe. Learners are taught never to share passwords with strangers, and to be cautious about sharing them even with friends. A password manager or a memorable but non-obvious personal method (e.g. a phrase turned into an acronym with substitutions) can help create and remember strong, unique passwords.

A computer virus is a type of malicious software (malware) that can copy itself and spread from one computer to another, often causing damage such as corrupting files, slowing down the computer, or stealing information. Viruses commonly spread through infected email attachments, downloaded files from untrusted sources, infected USB flash drives, and malicious websites. Antivirus software is a program designed to detect, block and remove viruses and other malware from a computer. Good practice includes: keeping antivirus software installed and regularly updated (since new viruses appear constantly), not opening attachments or links from unknown senders, and scanning external storage devices (like USB drives) before opening their files.

Cyber wellness refers to the safe, responsible, healthy and balanced use of ICT and online spaces. Key aspects include: protecting personal information online (not sharing full name, address, school, or phone number publicly), being respectful and kind in online communication (avoiding cyberbullying), recognising and reporting inappropriate content or contact to a trusted adult, balancing screen time with other healthy activities, and thinking critically about information found online rather than believing everything seen (since not all online information is accurate or trustworthy).

Computer software is broadly divided into two categories: system software (manages the computer's own hardware and provides a platform for other software to run, e.g. the operating system such as Windows, or Android on a phone) and application software (programs that let users perform specific tasks, e.g. a word processor for writing documents, a spreadsheet program for calculations, a web browser for browsing the internet, or a game). Understanding this distinction helps learners see that the operating system is what starts up when a device is switched on and manages everything else, while applications are the individual tools/programs opened to do particular jobs.

A spreadsheet is a grid of rows and columns used to organise, calculate and analyse data, made up of individual cells (each identified by a column letter and row number, e.g. cell B3). Basic spreadsheet concepts include: entering data (text, numbers, dates) into cells, using simple formulas to perform calculations (e.g. a formula that adds the values of two cells together), and creating charts/graphs from spreadsheet data to visualise it. Common uses at Junior level include recording and totalling simple data sets, such as class attendance, test scores, or a simple budget, connecting ICT skills directly to Mathematics data-handling skills.

Peripherals are devices connected to a computer that are not part of its core processing unit. Input devices allow a user to enter data or commands into a computer, e.g. keyboard, mouse, microphone, scanner, and webcam. Output devices allow a computer to present information to a user, e.g. monitor/screen, printer, speakers, and projector. Some devices, such as a touchscreen, act as both input (receiving touch commands) and output (displaying information) at the same time.
